meta.theme: lying against misleading: the defence that the hearer completes the inference fails once the sentence was chosen for that inference, and what survives is a difference in what the deceiver has staked, which matters where the standing of assertion needs protecting

meta.reviewer_notes: The hardest item of the batch. The passage destroys one defence of a distinction and then rebuilds a narrower one on a different footing, so every question turns on which of the two differences an option is talking about: the contribution to the false belief, which the author denies differs, or the exposure, which he says does.

quality.adversarial_review: The whole set turns on one separation, and the distractors are built out of readers who have not made it: the author denies that the two deceivers contribute differently to the false belief and affirms that they risk different things. Q1's live rival is the public defence the misleader retains, which is true of him and belongs to the fourth paragraph, where it is the author's own finding rather than the defence reported in the second. Q2's rival is the option that a narrowly answering witness does no damage a court need mind; the fifth paragraph says a court can survive such a witness, which is weaker, and the remedy it names is another question rather than an absence of harm. Q3's rival is the option that the regulator drew his own conclusion, which is the defence the third paragraph refuses in terms: responsibility follows choice, not utterance. Q4's rival is approval on the ground of a smaller contribution, which is approval for the reason the passage denies. Q5's rival is the condition about planning, which comes from the critique and not from the surviving difference. Q6's rival is the scene, which is vivid enough to read as the subject.

paragraphs.text: The investigator asked him where he had been on the Tuesday evening. He said that he had been at his sister's house until six, which was true; he had driven there after work, stayed for tea, and left when the clock in her hall struck the hour. The investigator wrote it down and moved on to the next question. What the investigator did not learn, and was not meant to learn, was that the warehouse stands eleven minutes from the sister's front door, and that the man arrived there at ten past seven. Nothing false had been said. A false belief had been produced, and produced deliberately, by a man who had spent some time before the interview deciding what to say.

Most people feel that this is not quite as bad as a flat denial, and philosophers have supplied the feeling with a justification. When you lie, you assert what you believe to be false, and the hearer's false belief is your work from beginning to end. When you mislead, you assert only truths; the hearer builds the false belief himself, out of an inference he was not compelled to draw. He assumed that a man accounting for his evening was accounting for all of it. You did not tell him that. On this account the misleader has left the last step to his victim, and that step, taken by the victim, is what separates the two cases. The distinction is not a lawyer's quibble, its defenders insist, but a difference in who did what.

The defence does not survive contact with the scene. The man did not blurt out a true sentence and then watch, helpless, while an inference formed in somebody else's head. He chose that sentence from among the true ones available to him, and he chose it because of the inference it would produce; had he expected the investigator to draw no conclusion from it, he would have said something else. Responsibility follows choice, not utterance. A person who arranges the conditions under which another will reason wrongly has done the thing he arranged, and crediting the victim with the final movement of his own mind is like calling a man innocent of a push because gravity did the falling. Whatever else is true of the distinction, it cannot be that the misleader has made the smaller contribution to the false belief.

Something does survive, but it is not what the defence claimed. Set the two men side by side after the interview. The liar has put his word behind a falsehood; if the truth comes out, what he said is worthless, and so, from then on, is anything else he says under the same conditions. The misleader has kept his word intact. Every sentence he uttered will survive checking, and he retains a defence he can offer in public, namely that he answered what he was asked. That is a real difference, and it is a difference in exposure rather than in guilt. The liar has spent something the misleader kept in reserve, and what he spent was not only his own comfort. It was the general standing of assertion, which the rest of us are drawing on whenever we take anybody's word for anything.

That is why the distinction earns its keep in courts and under oaths, and why it thins out at a kitchen table. An institution built on testimony has to protect the standing of assertion itself; it can survive a witness who answers narrowly, because the remedy for a narrow answer is another question, and it cannot survive witnesses whose sentences mean nothing, because for that there is no remedy at all. So the law draws its line where it does, and is right to. Between friends nothing of the kind is at stake. What is protected there is not the reliability of sentences but the confidence of one person in another, and that confidence is injured by the intention, which both men had, rather than by the form of words, which only one of them took trouble over. Anyone who has received a technically true answer from someone he trusted knows how little the technicality bought.

questions.target_mistake: answering with the difference the author himself establishes in the fourth paragraph instead of the one the defenders assert in the second
questions.stem: According to the passage, the standard defence of misleading holds that the two cases differ because

options.A: the misleader lacks the intention to deceive that the liar has
options.B: the harm done by a misleading answer is usually the smaller one
options.C: the hearer completes the false belief himself, by an inference he was not forced to draw
options.D: the misleader retains a defence that he can offer in public afterwards

explanation.expert_notice: The second paragraph states the defence and then names it twice over: the hearer builds the false belief himself, out of an inference he was not compelled to draw, and the misleader has left the last step to his victim. The closing sentence labels the whole thing a difference in who did what.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is that claim in plainer words. The defence is not about outcomes or motives but about agency: the liar performs the whole deception, whereas the misleader stops short and the victim supplies the rest. Everything the third paragraph then attacks is aimed at exactly this, which is why it matters to have taken the defence down accurately.
explanation.question_type_note: A detail question about a reported position is answered from the sentences that report it. Where a passage both reports a view and later supplies a better one, the decoys come from the better one.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author sets out a view he is about to attack, mark where the report ends. Questions on such passages are built at the seam, and material from the author's own account will be offered as though it belonged to the view he rejected.

distractors.why_wrong: Neither the defenders nor the author says anything of the kind, and the passage twice insists on the opposite: the false belief was produced deliberately, and the friendship case turns on the intention, which both men had.
distractors.seductive_element: A lesser offence is usually explained by a lesser intention, so the reader supplies the explanation the passage never gives.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage never sets the two harms side by side. Its defenders rest on who performed the deception and its author on what each deceiver put at risk, and neither party offers any comparison of how much damage was done.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does say that misleading feels not quite as bad, and a lesser feeling suggests a smaller harm.

distractors.why_wrong: These are the passage's own words, taken from the fourth paragraph, where the defence the misleader can offer in public belongs to the author's finding about exposure. Moved back two paragraphs they become a claim the defenders never made, since their case rests entirely on who took the last step.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival: a real feature of the misleader's position, stated in the passage, and easy to file under the earlier discussion of why his case is different.

questions.target_mistake: explaining the law's harsher treatment of the liar by a greater wrong to the person deceived, when the passage locates the difference outside the individual case altogether
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the reason will be institutional: what the liar damages is the credit of assertion, which is what a system of testimony cannot do without.
questions.stem: Which of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: The law treats the liar more harshly than the misleader because he does a greater injury to the particular person he has set out to deceive.
options.B: A witness who answers narrowly does no damage that a court needs to concern itself with.
options.C: The misleader's answer would be harmless in any setting where nobody was under oath.
options.D: The law's sharper treatment of the liar answers a harm to the standing of assertion rather than a greater wrong to the person deceived.

explanation.expert_notice: Two sentences have to be put together. The fourth paragraph says the liar spends the general standing of assertion, which the rest of us draw on whenever we take anybody's word; the fifth says an institution built on testimony has to protect that standing and that there is no remedy for witnesses whose sentences mean nothing. Meanwhile the third paragraph has already denied that the misleader contributes less to the false belief.
explanation.correct_reasoning: If the two deceivers do not differ in what they do to the person in front of them, the law's different treatment cannot be explained by that person's injury. What does differ is what each man puts at risk, and the passage says an institution of testimony must protect exactly that. So the line the law draws is a defence of the currency of assertion rather than a ranking of wrongs, and the correct option says so while keeping the denial the third paragraph established.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question at this level usually needs two paragraphs, not one. Look for an option that could only be built by joining a denial in one place to an affirmation in another.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author rules something out and then explains the same phenomenon in other terms, expect a question that offers the ruled-out explanation back. Keep the denial and the replacement side by side in your notes.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph forecloses it: whatever else is true of the distinction, it cannot be that the misleader has made the smaller contribution to the false belief. The difference the author allows is one of exposure rather than of guilt.
distractors.seductive_element: Harsher punishment ordinarily tracks a worse wrong, so the familiar explanation arrives before the passage's own has been noticed.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says a court can survive such a witness, and names the reason: the remedy for a narrow answer is another question. Being repairable is not the same as being harmless, and the same paragraph is at pains to say the technicality buys very little.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because survival and safety sit close together, and the paragraph does contrast the narrow answer favourably with the worthless sentence.

distractors.why_wrong: The last paragraph moves to settings with no oath precisely to say that the injury remains: between friends the confidence is damaged by the intention, which both men had, and the form of words buys almost nothing.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does say the distinction thins out away from the courtroom, and a reader hears thinning of the distinction as thinning of the offence.

questions.target_mistake: applying the defence the passage rejected instead of the two findings it keeps: equal contribution to the false belief, unequal exposure
questions.prediction_target: The learner should extract both findings first: the chosen true answer contributes as much as a false one would, and what the chooser keeps is a record that will survive checking.
questions.stem: A company asked by a regulator whether it has received complaints about a product replies with the exact number received in the past year, knowing that the regulator will take this for the total and that most complaints arrived the year before. On the passage's account, this reply

options.A: is less culpable than a false figure would have been, because the regulator drew the wrong conclusion himself from figures that were all accurate
options.B: contributes as much to the regulator's false belief as a false figure would, while leaving the company's statements able to survive checking
options.C: is worse than a false figure would have been, since it also exploits the regulator's trust in the company's candour
options.D: falls outside the passage's analysis, which concerns individual deceivers rather than institutions

explanation.expert_notice: The passage leaves the reader with two findings and they point in different directions. Contribution to the false belief: equal, since the sentence was chosen for the inference it would produce. Exposure: unequal, since every sentence the misleader uttered will survive checking. An applied case has to be assessed on both.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The company chose a true figure from among the true things it could have said, and chose it for the conclusion the regulator would draw, which is exactly the third paragraph's case; so nothing is subtracted from its contribution. At the same time it has not put its word behind a falsehood, and its answer will stand up if the file is examined, which is the fourth paragraph's surviving difference. The correct option keeps both halves and ranks neither above the other.
explanation.question_type_note: Application questions want the author's findings run on a case he never saw. Where an author reaches two findings, check the new case against both, since options are built by dropping one.
explanation.reading_habit: Before reading the options in an applied case, write the author's conclusions as a short list. An option that answers only one item on the list is the commonest wrong answer in this form.

distractors.why_wrong: This applies the defence the passage dismantles. The third paragraph answers it directly: responsibility follows choice, not utterance, and a person who arranges the conditions under which another will reason wrongly has done the thing he arranged.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the reasoning almost everybody brings to such a case, and the passage states it sympathetically before turning on it.

distractors.why_wrong: No ranking above the lie is available anywhere in the passage. The most it claims is that the misleader's contribution is not the smaller one, and its only asymmetry runs the other way, in what the liar has spent and the misleader kept.
distractors.seductive_element: A reader who has just watched a comfortable excuse demolished expects the verdict to keep going past equality.

distractors.why_wrong: Institutions are the setting of the argument's conclusion. The fifth paragraph is about what a system of testimony must protect, and it is there that the author says the distinction earns its keep.
distractors.seductive_element: The passage does open on one man in an interview room, and a reader who takes the scene for the scope reads the whole essay as a private morality.

questions.target_mistake: reading the demolition of the defence as contempt for the distinction itself, or the rescue of the distinction as agreement with the reason usually given for it
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: he thinks the usual justification is bad and the distinction nevertheless worth keeping, on a different and narrower ground.
questions.stem: The author's attitude towards the distinction between lying and misleading is best described as

options.A: unpersuaded by the usual justification of it, yet convinced that a narrower version survives
options.B: impatient with it as a piece of evasion dressed up as moral philosophy
options.C: approving, since it marks a real difference in how much each deceiver contributed
options.D: detached, setting out the arguments on each side without endorsing either of them

explanation.expert_notice: The passage passes two verdicts and both are unmistakable. The defence does not survive contact with the scene, and then, four sentences later, something does survive, but it is not what the defence claimed. An attitude question has to accommodate a refusal and a rescue in the same voice.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names both. The usual justification is rejected outright, with an argument and an analogy; the distinction is then rebuilt on a different footing, and the author goes so far as to say the law draws its line where it does and is right to. That is not indifference, not contempt, and not the approval the defenders were asking for.
explanation.question_type_note: Attitude questions are decided by what an author does rather than by the temperature of his sentences. Where a passage refuses a reason and keeps the conclusion, the attitude has two components and the answer must carry both.
explanation.reading_habit: Separate an author's view of an argument from his view of the thing the argument was about. Rejecting a bad defence of a practice is entirely compatible with defending the practice better.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage explicitly endorses the distinction where it matters, saying the law is right to draw its line, and it treats the defenders' position seriously enough to state it at length before answering it.
distractors.seductive_element: The third paragraph is severe and the last sentence is withering, so the reader takes the sharpest moment for the settled attitude.

distractors.why_wrong: The approval is real and the reason is the one the passage denies: it says in terms that it cannot be that the misleader has made the smaller contribution to the false belief. What differs is what each man staked, not what each did.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the near-tie, agreeing with the author's verdict while keeping the ground he cut away, which makes it read as a summary of the whole piece.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing here is neutral. One position is refuted with an analogy about a push and a fall, another is built in its place, and the law's practice is called right; an author who reaches three verdicts is not reporting.
distractors.seductive_element: The second paragraph is a fair and generous statement of the other side, which can read as even-handedness sustained throughout.

questions.target_mistake: borrowing the condition from the critique — that the sentence was chosen in advance — and attaching it to the difference the author allows
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: the difference allowed is about what is risked rather than what is done, and it matters only where the credit of assertion is the thing in need of protection.
questions.stem: Which of the following best states the limits the author places on the difference he allows between lying and misleading?

options.A: It holds only where the deceiver chose his words in advance, and not where a misleading answer was given on the spur of the moment without any planning at all.
options.B: It is a difference in what the deceiver has put at risk rather than in what he has done, and it tells where the reliability of assertion needs protecting.
options.C: It applies wherever a hearer is in a position to check what was said, which is to say almost everywhere.
options.D: It disappears once the deception is discovered, since both men are then known to have deceived.

explanation.expert_notice: The fourth paragraph states the difference and its category in one sentence: that is a real difference, and it is a difference in exposure rather than in guilt. The fifth then gives its range, court and oath on one side, the kitchen table on the other, with a reason attached to each.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option reports both limits and nothing else. The category is exposure, which keeps the third paragraph's denial intact, since nothing has been conceded about what the two men did. The range is set by what an institution needs: where the standing of assertion is what must be protected, the difference does work, and where the thing protected is one person's confidence in another, it does very little.
explanation.question_type_note: A scope question asks how far a claim reaches and on what condition. The answer is usually the sentence in which the author names the category of his own claim, not the sentence in which he states it.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author says a difference is real, read on for the noun he attaches to it. Guilt, exposure, degree, kind: the noun fixes the scope, and every scope question is decided by it.

distractors.why_wrong: Advance choice belongs to the third paragraph, where it is used to destroy the defence, not to the fourth, where the surviving difference is built. The misleader's word is intact whether or not he prepared, because what preserves it is that his sentences were true.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival: the deliberation before the interview is the passage's most emphasised fact, and a condition that prominent seems bound to qualify the conclusion.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage limits the difference by what is at stake in a setting, not by whether checking is possible. Between friends, where anything said can be checked easily, it says the difference thins out because sentences are not what is being relied on.
distractors.seductive_element: Checking really is the mechanism by which the misleader's word survives, so making checkability the condition feels like following the argument.

distractors.why_wrong: Discovery is when the difference becomes visible rather than when it vanishes: the passage describes the two men after the truth comes out, one with a worthless word and one with a record that survives checking and a defence he can offer in public.
distractors.seductive_element: Once both are known to have deceived, it seems obvious that any distinction between them has become academic.

questions.target_mistake: choosing the opening scene, which is the most memorable thing in the passage, as though it were the subject of the argument
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: a title has to name the surviving difference, which is about what each deceiver risked rather than about who said what.
questions.stem: Which of the following would be the most appropriate title for the passage?

options.A: Why Misleading Is Simply Lying by Another Name
options.B: An Answer That Was Entirely True
options.D: The Difference Is in What Is Staked

explanation.expert_notice: The passage spends one paragraph on a scene, two demolishing an explanation, and two building another. Whatever a title names has to be the thing the last two paragraphs are about, since that is where the argument ends and what the closing sentence is measuring.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct title is the author's own conclusion compressed. He denies that the two men differ in what they did and locates the difference in what each put at risk, and every later move follows from that: the liar spending the standing of assertion, the courtroom protecting it, the friendship having nothing of the sort to protect. A title that names the stake covers all five paragraphs at the altitude of the argument.
explanation.question_type_note: A title question is a main-idea question with a length limit. Test each option for altitude: too low and it names the example, too high and it names a claim the passage refused to make.
explanation.reading_habit: Ask what a title would have to leave out. The right one leaves out the scene and the applications; the wrong ones usually keep one of those and lose the argument.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage refuses this in its fourth paragraph, where something does survive and is called a real difference; only the defenders' explanation of the difference has been rejected, not the difference itself.
distractors.seductive_element: The third paragraph is so severe that it reads as an identification of the two offences, and the last sentence about the technicality seems to confirm it.

distractors.why_wrong: This names the opening scene, which is the passage's illustration rather than its subject; nothing in it points to the stake, the institution, or the difference in exposure on which the argument turns.
distractors.seductive_element: The scene is vivid, comes first, and is the thing a reader remembers, which is precisely how examples get promoted to theses.

distractors.why_wrong: Courts and oaths occupy part of one paragraph, as the setting where the surviving difference does the most work; the same paragraph moves to friendship, where the passage says it does very little.
distractors.seductive_element: It picks the passage's most concrete application and the one where the author most clearly commits himself, saying the law is right to draw its line there.

vocabulary.meaning_here: the bare act of saying something, considered apart from why it was said

vocabulary.passage_use: It was the general standing of assertion
vocabulary.meaning_here: the credit a thing is generally allowed, and on which others rely

vocabulary.passage_use: knows how little the technicality bought
vocabulary.meaning_here: a point of exact wording that changes nothing of substance

mentor.challenge: One defence of a familiar distinction is destroyed and another is built in its place. Keep the two apart, because almost every option in this set is the rejected one wearing the accepted one's clothes.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: A man who answers an investigator with a carefully chosen true sentence contributes as much to the false belief as a liar would, since he picked the sentence for the inference it would cause; what still separates him from a liar is not what he did but what he risked, which is why the distinction matters under oath and matters very little between friends.
mentor.main_idea: The usual defence of misleading says the hearer completes the deception himself. That fails, because the misleader chose his words for the conclusion they would produce. What survives is different: the liar stakes his word and can lose it, while the misleader keeps a record that will survive checking. That difference matters where a system depends on people's sentences being reliable, and hardly at all where what is at stake is one person's trust in another.
mentor.simple_explanation:
A man is asked where he was on Tuesday evening. He says he was at his sister's until six. That is completely true. He does not mention that he drove to the warehouse afterwards and arrived at ten past seven. Nothing false has been said, and the investigator now believes something false.

Most of us feel this is not as bad as simply denying he went. Philosophers explain the feeling like this: a liar creates the false belief himself, whereas a misleader only says true things and the listener jumps to the wrong conclusion on his own.

The writer says that explanation does not hold up. The man did not accidentally say a true sentence and watch in horror as a conclusion formed. He picked that sentence out of all the true ones he could have used, and he picked it because of the conclusion it would cause. If he had thought it would cause no conclusion, he would have said something else. You are responsible for what you choose, not merely for the words that came out. So the misleader did not contribute less.

But something else really does separate them. After the interview, look at the two men. The liar has put his word behind something false. When that is discovered, his word is worth nothing, and neither is anything else he says. The misleader still has his word. Every sentence he said checks out, and he can say in public that he answered the question he was asked. So the difference is not in what they did; it is in what each one risked.

That explains where the distinction matters. A court runs on testimony. It can cope with a witness who answers too narrowly, because you can ask another question. It cannot cope with witnesses whose sentences mean nothing, because there is no fix for that. So the law is right to treat lying as the worse thing.

Between friends there is no such machinery to protect. What matters there is whether one person can trust another, and that is damaged by the intention, which both men had. The clever wording buys almost nothing, as anyone who has been on the receiving end of a technically true answer already knows.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage builds a distinction, knocks it down, and then rebuilds it on a completely different foundation, and the two foundations are easy to confuse because both end in the sentence that misleading is not the same as lying. Readers who carry away only the conclusion will accept any option that gives a reason for it, including the reason the third paragraph destroyed. The fifth paragraph adds a second difficulty by making the distinction's importance depend on the setting, so that the same act is treated as significantly different in a courtroom and barely different at home.
mentor.author_intention: To take an excuse most people accept, show that it does not describe what the excuser actually did, and then find the smaller and stranger truth that the excuse was hiding.

paragraph_journey.note: A man answers an investigator with a true sentence that leaves out the part that matters. Nothing false is said, and a false belief is deliberately produced.
Lying creates the false belief from start to finish; misleading leaves the last step to the listener, who draws a conclusion nobody forced on him.
He chose that sentence because of the conclusion it would produce. Responsibility goes with the choice, so his contribution is not the smaller one.
The liar stakes his word and loses it if caught. The misleader's sentences all check out and he keeps a public defence. The difference is in exposure, not in guilt.
Courts must protect the reliability of testimony, so the line the law draws is right. Between friends what is damaged is trust, which the careful wording does not spare.

mentor.tone_progression: Flat and factual through the scene, generous while the defence is stated, sharp and unrelenting while it is taken apart, and then precise rather than triumphant, ending in a quiet line addressed to the reader's own experience.
key_transitions: 'The defence does not survive contact with the scene.' (opening of paragraph 3) — the reported justification is refused, and the refusal is argued rather than asserted.
'Something does survive, but it is not what the defence claimed.' (opening of paragraph 4) — the distinction is rebuilt on a new footing.
'That is why the distinction earns its keep in courts and under oaths, and why it thins out at a kitchen table.' (opening of paragraph 5) — the difference acquires a range.
mentor.misunderstanding: Readers finish this passage with one of two wrong pictures. The first is that the author has abolished the distinction, which the third paragraph seems to do and the fourth immediately undoes. The second, and the more expensive, is that he has kept the distinction along with its usual reason, so that misleading counts as a smaller contribution to the deception. He says the opposite in so many words. Everything he allows the misleader is about what happens afterwards, when somebody checks.
mentor.traps_summary: Three families recur. The rejected defence is offered back as the author's view, both directly and inside an applied case. The surviving difference is given the wrong category, so that exposure becomes guilt, or the wrong condition, so that it depends on having planned the answer. And the opening scene, which is the most memorable part of the passage, is offered as its subject in the title question.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author keeps a conclusion but throws away the reason usually given for it, write both down separately: conclusion kept, reason replaced. Almost every distractor in a passage of this shape is built by pairing the kept conclusion with the discarded reason, and the pairing is invisible unless the two were recorded apart. The habit also protects you in reverse, against options that take the demolished reason as a demolition of the conclusion.
mentor.real_world: Anyone who has written a reference, answered a due-diligence question, or explained a delay to a client has stood where this man stood, choosing among true sentences for the one whose effect they wanted, and the passage is a test of whether the choosing counts.
mentor.takeaway: Choosing the sentence for the conclusion it will produce makes the conclusion yours, whatever the words were.
mentor.reflection_question: When did you last say something entirely true in order that someone would believe something false?
